sweepcf · walkthrough for the team

One journey. One number changes. A different body shape is required.

Most datasets vary the scene. This one varies the decision the scene forces — and proves the difference in physics.

The problem, in one comparison

Put a robot's walk into fifty different rooms and you get fifty different images and one identical trajectory. That is useful visual augmentation, and it teaches a policy nothing about choosing behaviour, because the correct behaviour never changed.

So we build matched pairs instead. Below, the two motions share their route frame for frame, their duration, their gait phase, their start and their goal. They differ in exactly six leg joints. Then one shelf height decides which of them physics allows.

The 2×2, verified in simulation

The large video in each panel is a camera fixed in the room — the robot walks past it, so you can watch the gait and the body shape against a stationary background. Below it, a to-scale side view with the peak height and shelf marked, and the robot's own head camera from the same rollout.

Read the numbers on the panels

In the hard scene the walking robot peaks at 1.265 m against a shelf at 1.257 m — 8 mm of interference, and it is rejected. The crouch peaks at 1.228 m and passes with 29 mm to spare. Same room, same route, same controller: the only difference is the body shape the robot adopts for about a second.

What the robot itself sees

These are frames from the head camera on the failing run, plus the same instant when crouching. The obstacle is visible well before it is reached, which is what makes a decision possible rather than a lookup.

The rooms are deliberately untextured. This dataset is about geometry and feasibility, not photorealism — every claim it makes is about what the body can physically do, so the renderer is not where the effort goes.

How a family is built

  1. Qualify a motion. Start from a walk the controller already tracks successfully.
  2. Adapt it locally. A crouch is applied only around the obstacle, as a coupled squat — hip down 1, knee up 2, ankle down 1 — leaving the route, timing and the rest of the clip untouched. The waist does not move.
  3. Choose where the obstacle goes. At the point along the route where the two bodies differ most. Picking the route midpoint instead finds no usable families at all.
  4. Propose a window geometrically. Sweep each motion's collision volume against a descending shelf to get a candidate range of heights.
  5. Certify it in physics. Roll out to find where each motion really fails. Geometry proposes; only physics certifies.
  6. Accept the family only if all four cells come out as a counterfactual requires, and the failure is attributable to the intended obstacle.

Where this honestly stands

Proven: the mechanism. One matched family is fully verified in physics, and its failure is attributed to the shelf — contact at frame 90, loss of balance at 97, so the drift follows the collision rather than causing it. The outcome also survives three start-pose perturbations.

Not yet proven: that a learner trained on many such families chooses the right adaptation in a room it has never seen. That needs 24–30 verified families across at least 8 different walks; we have 1 matched family across 3 walks. Building those is the current work, and it is the whole point — the dataset is a means to that experiment.
